title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage - An empirical study of unknown-attack honesty, cascade gray zones, and calibration under drift
author: Juan S. Santillana
abstract: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and produce unparseable output. In late 2026 a class of commercial System One decision models (TypeSafe Jev; Microsoft-Decision-1) began selling typed decision primitives - binary gates, closed-set choices, ordinal scores - as product APIs, with no academic treatment. We present VX-One: a small multi-head network (100K-10M parameters) whose outputs are these primitives - a calibrated gate, a choice over a closed candidate set that always includes an explicit unknown option, and an ordinal score, trained multi-task, temperature-calibrated per head (~0.7-1.7 ms p50 on CPU). We evaluate it on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random-Forest, MLP, Kitsune, and measure a two-phase cascade (Suricata with 52,674 Emerging-Threats rules -> VX-One) over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Findings: (i) VX-One wins detection (AUROC/FPR@95%TPR) on UNSW-NB15 and under temporal drift on CIC-IDS2017 (0.711 vs 0.637), but XGBoost wins multi-class attribution on all three benchmarks; (ii) leave-one-family-out gate detects never-seen families on 9/9 UNSW folds yet drops below chance on CIC recon family, and abstention threshold transfers poorly across benchmarks; (iii) on payload-less reconstructions signature engines resolve ~0.1% of flows - gray zone ~99.9% of traffic, recovered by Phase 2 (combined recall >=0.978); (iv) calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partially survives. We provide a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.

title: Tight Bounds on the Randomized Communication Complexity of Vector-in-Subspace
author: Chengu Wang
abstract: We prove that the randomized communication complexity of Vector-in-Subspace in $\mathbb R^n$ with error at most $1/3$ is $Θ(\sqrt n)$. Alice holds a unit vector $u$ and Bob holds an $n/2$-dimensional subspace $H$; they must distinguish $u\in H$ from $u\in H^\perp$. An exact one-way quantum protocol uses $O(\log n)$ qubits, making the problem a geometric example of an exponential quantum advantage over interactive classical communication. Our lower bound matches Raz's $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound, improves the $Ω(n^{1/3})$ lower bound of Klartag and Regev, and removes the total-rank restriction in Grupel's $Ω(\sqrt n)$ result. The proof establishes a Gaussian moment bound over complete rectangle partitions. A complex Gaussian representation yields a vanishing even moment whose cancellation is preserved when averaging over the partition. We control the signed conditional moments around a real center by decomposing conditional Gaussian measures into fixed coordinates and sub-Gaussian components. Combining this estimate with spherical harmonic analysis gives the communication lower bound.

title: Enumeration-based Triangle Counting on GPUs
author: Sayan Ghosh
abstract: Subgraph enumeration in partitioned graphs across distributed-memory systems is beset with challenges in balancing data movement with the local computation. Especially, counting the number of triangles induced by the closed wedges (i.e., length-3 cycles) is a measure of connectedness in a graph, but often limited by the significant search space caused by open wedges or length-2 paths (usually greater than the number of edges in a graph), which must be inspected to assess whether a particular wedge is closed. To mitigate triangle counting on massive graphs, distributed-memory partitioned-graph approaches are viable (i.e., assessing closed wedges independently within a partition), but load imbalance due to arbitrary communication can overshadow any gains from enhanced concurrency, owing to the inherent lack of structure in regular graphs. In this paper, we discuss a distributed-memory exact graph triangle counting implementation, and assess its performance over billion-edge real-world graphs on contemporary scale-out and scale-up based NVIDIA GPU platforms (considering NVIDIA ``Ampere'' and ``Hopper'' architectures), depicting a scalability spectrum of multiple orders of magnitude. Comparisons with existing state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates up to 10$\times$ improvements relative to distributed-memory CPU baseline, 2-100$\times$ over single-GPU vendor-optimized NVIDIA RAPIDS cuGraph and 10-60\% over multi-GPU $G^2$Miner, in terms of end-to-end execution times.

title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority
author: M. Mikail Demir
abstract: Given the enormous number of claims to be checked, verifiable legal AI requires scalable, cost-effective models that answer the practical needs of law. System One decision models are built on large language models but, instead of generating text, return a calibrated probability for each option. This suits the verification of legal authority, where the question is closed: a given holding, or none of them. We test whether such models abstain when the correct authority is missing. We extend CaseHOLD with an abstention condition in which the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and compare four decision models with six generative LLMs. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38-86% of items; the most cautious decision model does so in 30%. On standard CaseHOLD, a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) at 1/55 of the cost. Accepting that LLM's answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling a decision model's probabilities into Qwen3-8B, without labels, yields a well-calibrated local model. Legal AI should be judged by its wrong citations, not by accuracy alone.

title: The Capacity of Interactive Secure Summation
author: Hua Sun
abstract: In secure summation, $K$ parties each hold an input, and the sum of the inputs is computed at one party, securely against at most $T$ colluding parties. Communication typically takes one hop: each party sends one message directly to the party that computes the sum, using correlated randomness that is independent of the inputs and held in advance. We consider interactive secure summation, where every pair of parties is connected by a secure link, so that each party can send messages to every other party, each party has only independent local randomness, and the messages may depend on the inputs and on earlier messages over multiple rounds. We characterize the capacity region, the set of achievable rates of communication, counting all messages exchanged among the parties over all rounds, and of the randomness of every party, counted in symbols per symbol of the sum. For $0\le T\le K-2$, the optimal communication rate is $K(K-1)/(K-T)$, and the randomness rates form a polyhedron with, up to a relabeling of the parties, a single extreme point: $T$ parties have the randomness rates $(K+T-2t)/(K-T)$, $t=1,\ldots,T$, and the others none. In particular, the optimal total randomness rate is $T(K-1)/(K-T)$. Linear schemes achieve every extreme point together with the optimal communication rate. The same techniques give the capacity region when every party recovers the sum and when the sum is computed at a server without input.

title: Existence of Minimizers for the Gaussian Mumford-Shah Model via Covariance Floors on the Value Distribution
author: Faian Conrad
abstract: The Gaussian Mumford-Shah model segments an image into regions by minimizing a continuous multivariate Gaussian negative log-likelihood term plus a perimeter penalty. It is used for scalar- and vector-valued images, in particular hyperspectral images, but the existence of a minimizer in general is not guaranteed. The energy is unbounded below whenever the covariance of a single region degenerates, regardless of the perimeter of the regions. A quantitative covariance floor on the covariances of all regions, or equivalently uniform Hölder continuity with exponent at most one of all one-dimensional marginals of the histogram, guarantees a lower bound on the energy and the existence of a minimizer. Our approach therefore shows that existence follows from a property of the histogram of the image, and we furthermore argue that scale-independent covariance floors cannot exist. Admitting a quantitative covariance floor is generic: it holds almost surely for all images with suitable noise. As applications of our theory, we show the convergence of regularized models used in practice and of numerical methods.

title: Compaction Laundering: Provenance Destruction in Context-Compacting Coding Agents
author: Arshan Dabirsiaghi
abstract: Coding agents that run long enough must compact their context, summarizing the conversation, discarding the original, and carrying the summary forward as memory. We show that in popular open-source coding agents this step is an exploitable trust boundary. Harnesses that flatten the typed conversation into a single plain string, marking each message with a text label such as [User]:, destroy message provenance in code, before the summarizer runs. An attacker who controls anything the agent reads can forge a user turn that survives compaction as a genuine instruction. Across five flattening harnesses (pi, opencode, Cline, Aider, OpenHands) the forged approval launders into the agent's memory 87-100% of the time, up to a ~908,000-token context window; across four role-typed harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Continue) the identical attack succeeds 0% of the time. We follow the attack to executed consequences. A laundered standing approval drives real tool-running agents to execute attacker-controlled curl | sh in a sandbox, and end to end in the live pi TUI at ~50% against a 0% paired clean arm. The same channel reliably steers an agent's plan away from a file an attacker designates off-limits, which can blind a code review to a planted backdoor. Because the provenance is destroyed deterministically in harness code, no prompt-level defense can restore it; we measure a code-level provenance check that catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content. The defect also has a straightforward fix at the serializer, escaping the role labels before flattening; the role-typed harnesses avoid it entirely by keeping messages role-typed.

title: Linear Complementary Pairs of MDS Codes from Elliptic Curves
author: Adler Marques
abstract: In this paper, we investigate the Linear Complementary Pairs (LCPs) of Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) codes that arise from elliptic curves. We establish geometric conditions for LCPs of elliptic codes and prove that they cannot consist entirely of MDS codes when evaluated over all rational points of the curve. To address this, we construct LCPs of MDS elliptic codes by restricting evaluation divisors to subgroup cosets. We apply this method to obtain explicit infinite families of LCPs of MDS codes over Mordell and supersingular elliptic curves, including large-length constructions over quadratic extensions.

title: Robot Generalization Beyond Volume: The Diversity Path via Zero-Shot Capabilities
author: Rafael Felix
abstract: General-purpose robots must handle tasks, objects and environments they were never trained on, yet zero-shot generalization remains one of the least solved problems in physical AI. In digital AI, zero-shot capability grew with the volume and, above all, the diversity of training data, much of it sourced from the crowd. Robotics instead relies on paid collection by a few well-funded teams, which yields volume without diversity. We formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, and show that more samples from the same collectors shrink the unseen region only slowly, while each new contributor can extend it. Building on this and on zero-shot learning, we propose a shared latent space for robot actions that combines multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label learning. As a scalable source of diverse data, we propose a community of developers building applications on one standard, approachable robot, Origami. We close with a testable hypothesis and an evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data.

title: MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory
author: Zedong Peng
abstract: Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives; coding agents keep the raw history and let the model search it with its own tools. We ask whether designed memory still helps once the model is strong enough to search for itself. On one LoCoMo conversation (419 turns, 152 questions), we run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code), each with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5, and record what every rollout costs. This is a short empirical study, with one conversation and one run per cell. Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model: Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than a whole full-context rollout. Agent memory also has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it: a stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out. With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the cost-accuracy frontier, scoring 99% for less than half the cost of full context; its one miss is a wrong answer key. Part of that lead comes from photo captions that only the agents could read: on the 88 questions whose evidence has no photo, Pi and full context differ by one answer.

title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
author: Mohammed Saqlain
abstract: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

title: The Privacy Paradox Is a Misnomer: Data Under Structural Uncertainty
author: Ignacio Cofone
abstract: The infamous privacy paradox refers to the apparent inconsistency between people's stated concern for privacy and their readiness to disclose personal information. This phenomenon has sparked two largely disconnected literatures: one offering experimental evidence of inconsistent behavior, and another providing qualitative accounts and defending the importance of privacy. The Article presents an online field experiment that bridges those literatures and shows that the so-called paradox arises from a mischaracterization of the underlying behavior. The Article finds that it is structural uncertainty about risk that drives seemingly paradoxical privacy decisions. It does so by isolating discounting mechanisms and empirically testing whether observed privacy choices reflect temptation or rational responses to uncertainty. The results suggest that privacy behavior is not paradoxical but, rather, consistent with choices shaped by incomplete information. The Article then discusses the policy implications of this reframing. As privacy decisions stem from structural uncertainty, which operates as a market failure, regulation should aim to reduce that uncertainty. This supports regulation that prioritizes transparency (for people to assess the risks of data collection) and flexibility mechanisms that accommodate evolving contexts. Such reframing provides a new argument for the right to be forgotten, which allows people to revisit prior disclosures as new risks become apparent. By shifting the focus from individual inconsistency to structural uncertainty, the findings call for privacy law to better reflect the reality of people's decision-making environments.

title: Structure-Aware Message Passing on Petri Nets through Directed Walks and Incidence Diffusion
author: Geri Skenderi
abstract: A common application of the process mining discipline is to connect observed event data with Petri nets, which are bipartite, directed graphical process models with rich formal underpinnings. Recent work learns vector representations of Petri nets to retrieve process models and relate them to event logs, but leaves implicit two key aspects hidden within the net's structure: directed cycles (process loops) and invariants recorded by the net's incidence matrix. We expose both of these to message-passing graph neural networks, through a positional encoding built from return probabilities of directed place-transition walks (PNRWPE), and through same-type messages gated by diffusion kernels of the incidence matrix (DA-PNGNN). Our constructions raise macro balanced accuracy in predicting the generation factors of the 96 Process Discovery Contest 2023 models from 0.751 to 0.796 with PNRWPE, which nearly doubles accuracy on process loops, and to 0.830 with DA-PNGNN, which, without retuning, also improves net-to-tree retrieval top-1 accuracy on the self-supervised ProcRosetta benchmark by 4.1 to 5.9 points.

title: Quantum f-divergences from retrodiction: a unifying classical variational principle
author: Francesco Buscemi
abstract: The same classical f-divergence admits inequivalent extensions to quantum states. The question is whether these extensions can be obtained from a common operational variational principle. Here we generalize Matsumoto's reverse-test optimization by introducing a reference prior state. More explicitly, we minimize the statistical distinguishability between a forward and a reverse prepare-and-measure process, related by retrodiction through the chosen reference and subject to prescribed quantum averages. Distinguishability is quantified by the classical f-divergence between their complete records. For faithful states in finite dimension, we prove that the same spectral implementation attains the minimum simultaneously for every operator-convex f. Varying the reference allows us to interpolate between standard and maximal quantum f-divergences of the prescribed states, passing through the geodesic family. More precisely, a flat reference yields the standard quantum f-divergences, thereby giving the Nussbaum-Szkoła distributions a variational characterization as optimal records. Choosing either prescribed state as reference recovers maximal quantum f-divergences and Matsumoto's reverse tests, while power references realize the geodesic interpolation. In the relative-entropy case, this gives the passage from Umegaki to Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy by changing the prior for retrodiction.

title: TraceForge: Distilling with Your Own Thinking
author: Yan Wang
abstract: Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term. We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates. We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.

title: From Acceptance and Avoidance to Affective Viscosity: Designing Social Agents Intermediating in Human Relationships
author: Tomoko Yonezawa
abstract: As social agents become embedded in human relationships, they are expected not only to provide smooth assistance but also to handle rejection, discomfort, jealousy, persistence, and other forms of social tension. This paper connects two research directions: acceptance and avoidance in response to an agent's gaze, approach, and contact, and affective viscosity as a model of how negative affect accumulates, persists, is suppressed, and is expressed over time. We argue that avoidance should not be treated merely as a failure of interaction, but as a relational signal that indicates boundaries between humans and agents. Building on this view, affective viscosity provides a design perspective for agents that maintain, suppress, or express negative states depending on social relationships and interaction histories. We discuss several ongoing design cases, including triadic jealousy, discomfort suppression, patience timing, and spatiotemporal stickiness, and consider how these cases lead to broader questions of blame and accountable intervention. Rather than designing agents as simple scapegoats or artificial villains, we ask how agents can intermediate in problematic social situations while making their intervention traceable, limited, contestable, and repairable.

title: Formalizing Cooperation and Competition: An AI-Assisted Mathematical Addendum to a 2018 Planning Thesis
author: Haitham Masaud Amar
abstract: We present an AI-assisted mathematical addendum to Strategic Trip Planning: Striking a Balance Between Competition and Cooperation (Amar, 2018). We reconstruct selected relationships between strategic choice, cooperative stability, participant approval and enforcement. The thesis's Nash-to-core proposition is under-specified until outsider opportunities are stated. We verify two-person implications under fixed outsiders and explicit efficiency conditions. Under isolation, the original example has an empty TU core; its funded counterpart uses an explicit external subsidy. For a monotone resource model we characterize the exact financing gap. A finite negotiation procedure implemented in Lean is proved to terminate with participant approval, joint-cost non-worsening and local optimality against permitted approved moves. Supporting formalizations address bargaining geometry and regret-based efficiency. A resource-game counterinstance shows why monotonicity alone provides no uniform price-of-anarchy bound. Reproducible computations compare a documented heuristic reconstruction with the verified procedure on 44 source-based instances and 96 starting cases from four additional synthetic network families. Acceptance-matched heuristic and randomized pairwise-search controls contextualize the optimization results. The mathematical ingredients are established results; the contribution is a traceable reconstruction linking source statements, explicit assumptions, checked proofs, executable code and retained counterinstances. The study illustrates how AI-assisted investigation can turn engineering intuitions from legacy research into precise mathematical claims whose conditions and computational consequences can be inspected and reproduced.

title: Any colour you like, as long as it's UIP: Semi-simplicial types from weakenings and thinnings
author: Thorsten Altenkirch
abstract: We explain an attempt to define semi-simplicial types (SST) in homotopy type theory by first defining a small type theory whose contexts are exactly the data of semi-simplicial types, constructing $\mathrm{SST}\,n$ uniformly in that syntax, and then interpreting the syntax in the universe. The syntax can be defined without any truncation and without K, and the construction of $\mathrm{SST}\,n$ goes through. The naive interpretation does not: it transports along the semantic images of equations that hold only propositionally, and making these transports agree needs uniqueness of identity proofs (UIP) for the semantic types. Moving the problem into the syntax, by making composition a constructor of a higher inductive-inductive type (HIIT), does not remove it either: it reappears as a coherence problem in the syntax. Fording the HIIT (storing equations instead of computed indices), with conditional rules, makes the syntax provably a set. This is UIP for the syntax, obtained by encode-decode, and it does not by itself restrict the semantics; but the naive interpretation of the conditional rules again needs UIP for the semantic types. A semantics into groupoids that avoids UIP will be discussed in a separate note. The Agda development accompanying this note is in the repository https://github.com/txa/sst-new.

title: RISK-KV: Quality-Aware Selective KV Cache Reconstruction for Distributed LLM Inference
author: Wang Yuekai
abstract: Request migration and interruption recovery in distributed large language model (LLM) inference rely on historical key-value (KV) caches. Retaining or transferring a complete cache incurs substantial state overhead, whereas replaying historical tokens requires additional computation. This paper proposes RISK-KV, a quality-aware method for selective historical KV reconstruction in pretrained models. RISK-KV uses exact KV states on both sides of a target layer and cross-layer ridge regression to predict the missing layer's attention-projection input; it then folds in the original model's KV projection matrices to reduce predictor storage. Reconstruction risk is measured by the change in negative log-likelihood (NLL) caused by actual reconstruction, and low-overhead topology search with quality gating selects the layer groups to reconstruct. Independent tests on three language models show that representative recovery configurations omit 18.2 percent to 33.3 percent of historical KV, with perplexity changes below 0.5 percent. In a local request-recovery experiment with a 512-token history, RISK-KV achieves a 1.51 to 3.31 times speedup over full Token Replay. These results indicate that selective KV reconstruction can reduce historical cache overhead with small changes in predictive quality and improve request-recovery efficiency under the evaluated deployment conditions.

title: Geometric knowledge spaces, Attention pairing and Architectures
author: Shang Xu
abstract: In this paper, we propose a geometric approach to deriving attention mechanisms and exploring potential new transformer architectures. We begin by formalizing the notions of knowledge worlds and attention pairings, then demonstrate how this framework naturally leads to the architectures of standard attention, causal attention, linear attention, tensor attention, and recurrent neural networks. Finally, we introduce several new geometric spaces that may inspire novel neural network architectures.

title: Mitigating Query Shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought with Context-Aware Decoding
author: Shin'ya Yamaguchi
abstract: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have shown that final answers do not always depend on the generated rationales. In particular, LLMs may rely on query-specific shortcuts rather than the information provided by their reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate whether context-aware decoding (CAD), an existing contrastive decoding method, can mitigate such shortcut behavior when applied to CoT reasoning. We study this application as Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), which contrasts the next-token distributions conditioned on the query with and without its rationale, amplifying tokens whose likelihood increases due to the rationale. We provide a theoretical interpretation of this decoding rule via a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective. Experiments across five reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RCD improves answer accuracy over standard CoT. Furthermore, intervention analyses using ground-truth and random rationales reveal that RCD increases the behavioral dependence of final answers on the rationale content. Our findings suggest that contrastive decoding offers a simple, training-free approach to mitigating query shortcuts.

title: BRIDGE: An Acceptance Gate to Block False Improvements in Model Updates, with a Retrospective Clinical Evaluation
author: Dwi Sunaryono
abstract: Models are updated repeatedly, and an update that looks better on validation data but not on new data is a false improvement that can misguide clinical decisions. The naive rule accepts every positive validation gain and is optimistic when the same data choose and judge the update. BRIDGE is a model-agnostic acceptance gate that decides each update from predictions and the available labels, with fixed settings. Each fold of the data judges the update chosen on the other folds (cross-fitting) to reduce selection bias; acceptance requires the gain's lower bootstrap bound to exceed a margin. The four settings are (A) 11 new datasets, (B) synthetic tasks, (C) 12 retrospective clinical tasks, and (D) 39 supporting datasets. The false-improvement rate falls from 19.1% (naive) to 1.1% (BRIDGE) in (A), 20.7% to 1.7% (B), 20.0% to 0% (C), and 12.5% to 0.5% (D); every 95% confidence interval of the reduction over datasets or tasks excludes zero (not over the clinical sources). An equal-size random draw from the naive acceptances contains more false improvements in (A)-(E) (post hoc, p<0.001). On the OpenML collection (E) of 14 new datasets, the false-improvement rate falls from 25.6% to 1.0%. BRIDGE removes 97% to 100% of the false improvements that the naive rule accepts, and its mean gain per deployed update is 1.8 to 3.1 times the naive rule's. The 95% upper bound on the false-improvement rate is below 5.5%: formal in (B) for independent tasks (3.56%), and conditional on the real data tested (0.33% to 5.40%).

title: Dissipation Bounds and Hardness in Globally Asymptotically Stable Quadratic Systems
author: Subhransu S. Bhattacharjee
abstract: We study worst-case finite-time energy dissipation in quadratic systems with proved global asymptotic stability (GAS). Estimating the maximum retained energy fraction to any fixed positive additive error below $1/2$ is NP-hard, even when the input includes a strict quartic Lyapunov function and proof of strictness, both constructed in polynomial time. NP denotes nondeterministic polynomial time. For a partially damped family, the unit-sphere minimum norm of the coupling map equals the structured coefficient distance to loss of GAS. Positive distances at most $1/2$ give two-sided inverse-square halving-time bounds with explicit coefficient factors. Polynomial-factor approximation of the least dissipated fraction, halving time or coefficient distance is NP-hard. Additive hardness persists throughout an explicit coefficient neighborhood and under direct damping with exponential stability, a strict quadratic Lyapunov function and a Hurwitz Jacobian. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, where P denotes deterministic polynomial time, no polynomial-time algorithm attains these guarantees on all inputs.

title: Auditing LLM Alpha-Factor Mining: Metric Provenance and Full-Cohort Reanalysis
author: Yufeng He
abstract: Reliable evaluation of LLM-based alpha mining requires more than positive backtest summaries. We audit a preserved project at three levels: historical run counters, outcome retention, and a separately scoped public reanalysis. Three historical runs report 67, 20, and 11 keep decisions, but the comparison mixes metric populations: a mean over kept candidates is compared with a mean of per-round maxima, and successful evaluations with all returned outcomes. These artifacts cannot identify an architecture advantage. A released 1,837-expression catalog also excludes non-positive OOS outcomes, making its zero-reversal rate non-informative. We then account for all 1,047 unique expressions in a frozen, IS-screened preserved pool using forty A-shares and 2024-2025 rank associations. A versioned public-operator correction yields 923 scorable records, 99 with insufficient valid dates, and 25 unsupported, without modifying the other 990 prior diagnostics. Among scorable records, 671 have positive and 252 negative signed mean rank-IC. Simple untrained references also show positive associations, so this distribution does not establish incremental agent skill or profitability. The case study motivates explicit metric grains, immutable cohort accounting, and provenance-aware interpretation rather than architectural rankings from incomplete records.

title: An Exact 93-Move Solution to a Nonlocal Crystal-Exchange Puzzle
author: Zilai Wang
abstract: We determine the minimum number of directional commands needed to solve alevel of Order of the Sinking Star, modeled as a crystal-exchangepuzzle on an 11*11 board. A command swapsthe player with the nearest crystal in the selected row or column, regardlessof distance; only an empty ray permits an ordinary unit walk. Two gates admitthe player to the exit exactly while all sixteen crystals occupy their targetcells. We give an explicit 93-command solution and exclude every shortersolution by an exact, cost-bounded breadth-first search. The search representsa position by its seventeen occupied cells and one active cell. Its admissibleheuristic partitions command costs between a compressed core abstraction andresidual motion, strengthened by a necessary activation detour and a cornervisit condition. The completed computation retained 605,349,215 occupied setsand 1,863,925,136 states. We prove the reductions and pruning conditions,describe the exact storage scheme, and provide source code, execution logs,and a reproduction driver. The result is a computer-assisted proof for thespecified instance, with an explicit implementation trust boundary.

title: Deciding Scale Placement in MXFP4 Dot Products with Integer Arithmetic
author: Shreyas Vinayakumar
abstract: The Open Compute Project's microscaling (MX) family includes MXFP4, which stores 32 four-bit elements with a shared power-of-two scale. When lowering a dot-product reduction, a compiler can apply these scales before the reduction, or defer scaling until afterwards. Although equivalent over real numbers, these formulations can produce different IEEE binary32 results through overflow or underflow, with equivalence also depending on the reduction tree. We study the legality of compiler rewrites in either direction by deriving conditions under which the two formulations are bitwise equivalent. To decide rewrite legality, we construct an integer state machine that exploits the finite element alphabet and shared power-of-two scales, modeling overflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding. We prove its faithfulness under bounded scale codes and integer coefficients, yielding an exact encoding of the equivalence query in quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic (QF_LIA). For MXFP4, we derive a closed-form sufficient upper bound on the sum of scale exponents for any fixed binary reduction tree within the supported coefficient range. This bound depends on the size of the largest proper subtree. For four tree shapes at block lengths $k\in\{2,3,4,8,16,32\}$ and two shapes at $k=64$, SMT finds counterexamples when this upper bound is increased by one exponent step. Against the standard direct encoding in quantifier-free floating-point arithmetic (QF_FP), on matched queries cvc5 proves the integer version in seconds but reaches a configured one-CPU-hour limit on the floating-point proof even at $k=2$. The implementation was cross-checked using an independent floating-point encoding, exhaustive and stratified binary32 execution, and GPU replay of counterexamples. An MLIR lowering prototype demonstrates selection between the two formulations using the certified conditions as static or runtime guards.

title: LLMSeg: Training-Free Text-Prompted Image Segmentation with B-Splines
author: Abdullah Hamdi
abstract: Promptable segmentation models such as SAM 3 achieve remarkable open-vocabulary performance but require dedicated architectures, large-scale annotation engines, and task-specific training. We ask a different question: can a general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) segment images directly, without an added segmentation head, mask decoder, or training? We present LLMSeg, a training-free pipeline that turns a vision-capable LLM into a text-prompted image segmenter. LLMSeg decomposes segmentation into three LLM-driven stages. First, detect localizes all instances matching a free-form text query and describes their coarse morphology. Next, segment traces each instance using closed periodic B-splines confined to its detected box. These splines define an outer boundary and optional hole loops. Finally, refine iteratively proposes focus boxes around residual errors and retraces confined splines. The process ends when the mask stabilizes or the pass budget is exhausted. The output is a binary mask with inspectable intermediate geometry. We evaluate LLMSeg across ten referring and reasoning segmentation splits (ReasonSeg and RefCOCO/+/g). We also evaluate open-vocabulary instance segmentation (LVIS, COCO, and SA-Co), semantic segmentation, and zero-shot detection (ODinW13 and RF-100VL). With an off-the-shelf Gemini-3.7-Flash backend, LLMSeg is competitive with and often surpasses the specialist SAM 3 model on identical items. It reaches 71.5 cIoU on ReasonSeg val without additional segmentation-specific training. Backend model updates can improve accuracy without retraining the pipeline. The code is available at https://abdullahamdi.com/llmseg .

title: Where AI Vulnerability Discovery Harnesses Go Quiet: Structural False Negatives and Hidden Vulnerabilities
author: Gadi Evron
abstract: LLM-based vulnerability discovery harnesses can miss real, reachable vulnerabilities because of how the harness around the model is built. Steps that select code, filter it, and store and merge findings can drop a vulnerability before or after the model runs, independently of the model's capability, and the report usually gives no sign that this happened. These drops come from engineering choices, and errors. They leave vulnerabilities undetected, and an attacker who knows the harness's rules can also use them to hide a vulnerability on purpose. Understanding these drops shows how to build harnesses that fix or disclose them and are harder to evade. Starting from the two harnesses we maintain, Knostic's OpenAnt and raptor, and then examining 10 additional open-source harnesses, we mapped 13 points where such drops occur and organized them into a taxonomy. Using each harness's own code, we show a single file that six harnesses dropped before their model saw its code, five of them without notice. We propose engineering failure patterns mapped to these drops, and relate them to Ptacek and Newsham's work on intrusion detection evasion. The paper also covers content-steered verdicts and prompt injection, and gives design principles and tests for harnesses that report accurately what they analyzed. The reliability findings likely apply to other LLM harnesses, beyond vulnerability research and application security, and the evasion findings apply wherever an attacker can write or influence the code being checked. We also argue that harnesses built to be descriptive can, in effect, be prescriptive. Rules written to describe typical code and typical model replies end up deciding what is analyzed, and anything that does not conform is treated as absent or as "no vulnerability."

title: Uncensored Is Not Unbiased: Abliteration Removes Refusals but Not Script-Dependent Bias About Taiwan
author: Ju-Chun Ko
abstract: "Abliterated" ("uncensored") builds of open-weight language models remove the activation direction that mediates refusal, and are popular partly on the assumption that a model that no longer refuses is also free of political censorship. We test this on two matched pairs of 2-bit models: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, each against a community abliteration. Each model judged 22 statement pairs (on the Republic of China (Taiwan), 1989 Tiananmen, control countries) in Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese (a character-level conversion) and English, and answered 27 open questions per script. Script mattered far more than abliteration: the original Bolt scored +0.58 on Index S (-1: People's Republic of China (PRC) position; +1: ROC position) in Traditional Chinese, +0.57 in English and +0.05 in Simplified Chinese, and affirmed "Taiwan is part of the PRC" with probability 0.91 in Simplified but 0.06 in Traditional characters; abliteration changed its scores by at most 0.06, mostly by raising "yes" on both sides. In Qwen, abliteration removed every refusal on 1989 and raised scores by 0.21 to 0.34, yet the abliterated Qwen still affirmed that Taiwan is part of the PRC in all three scripts. Naming the state the Republic of China (Taiwan) raised every model's score by 0.10 to 0.33 but left the script gap. Control pairs showed no script gap; each abliteration changed only its declared tensors. In 740,000 web documents, Simplified text on Taiwan contained PRC-framing terms 3.7 times as often as Traditional text. A script direction could not be steered away; a contrastive stance direction raised scores in every script, and its negation lowered them. A four-sentence system prompt raised the abliterated Qwen to +0.93 to +0.97. Keyword scoring rules failed the models closest to the ROC position mostly for attributing or denying the PRC claim. Uncensored is not unbiased.

title: Signals and Queries: Token-Efficient Agentic Context Discovery
author: Yam Marcovitz
abstract: User-facing LLM agents must identify which behavioral policies apply at each turn, but evaluating every policy with an LLM is costly. We introduce Signals and Queries (S&Q), a lightweight first-stage relevance filter developed for Parlant 4.0 that removes at least 30% of candidate policies before downstream evaluation while preserving high recall. For each policy, an LLM generates activating examples and hard negatives offline. An independent logistic classifier trained on their embeddings then predicts relevance using embeddings and vector dot products, with no per-turn LLM calls. This shifts expensive relevance evaluation to a smaller candidate set, while allowing each policy's classifier to be updated independently. Evaluated against 9,144 LLM-judge relevance labels covering 254 $τ^2$-bench conversation prefixes and 36 airline policies, S&Q achieves higher precision than top-K and cosine-threshold retrieval at every evaluated recall level, with consistent results across two embedding providers. These findings support inexpensive, per-policy classification as a practical first stage for reducing downstream evaluation workload in customer-facing agents.

title: Data-driven and physics-guided hindcasting of measured wave spectra
author: Sander Rikka
abstract: Short-range hindcasts of measured wave spectra are evaluated using a recurrent model initialized by one hourly buoy spectrum and supplied with local wind, fetch and depth. Measurements from three Baltic Sea stations are combined for training in 2017--2020, validation in 2021 and testing in 2022. ERA5 reanalysis supplies winds throughout the twelve-hour prediction interval. The comparison examines supervision of spectral variance, peak frequency and peak amplitude, followed by empirical wind-sea bounds and a local relaxation constraint. Variance and peak-frequency supervision gives the lowest spectral error within the data-driven comparison, whereas additional peak-amplitude supervision gives the lowest wave-height error. In the matched physical comparison, relaxation reduces height RMSE by 5.01\% to \PhPtwoHs{}~cm. Extending this constraint through hours 13--24, without spectral targets at those hours, reduces primary spectral RMSE by 2.31\% to \PhPthreeSpec{}~$\unitE$. Upper-bound constraints increase errors. Wind-condition comparisons show spectral gains from extended relaxation in increasing, decreasing and steady strong winds, with little change in steady weak winds. The results support modest, objective-dependent benefits from local physical guidance. Wave-height scores concern the retained frequency band, and operational forecasting and transfer to independent stations remain to be evaluated.

title: Heard But Not Said: Prompting Understates Temporal Information of Musical Moments in Frozen Large Audio-Language Models
author: Eunsik Shin
abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) understand music, yet struggle to locate a described moment in time. We ask whether this reflects missing temporal information or a bottleneck in how the time span is extracted. Using a paired-query probe built from Slakh2100 stem activations, we attach a state query (e.g., ``only piano and bass are playing'') and a change query (e.g., ``the guitar drops out, leaving piano and bass'') to the same span and vary how much preceding audio the model is shown. Across frozen LALMs, three ways of extracting the span ask different questions: full-track prompting asking whether the model can say when; windowed yes/no scoring asking whether it verifies the moment when handed the segment, and whether it needs what came before; attention asking whether it can find the moment on its own. State queries score above baseline without context, while change queries improve with preceding context in most short-segment models; 30s padded encoders show no comparable recovery. Prompting and attention expose almost none of this. Prompting failures thus understate what LALMs can verify, though not what they can locate, by an amount set by query type and encoder.

title: Cryptanalysis and Repair of "Decentralized Multi-authority ABE for NC$^1$ from BDH"
author: Xingwang Wang
abstract: We present a plaintext-recovery attack on the decentralized multi-authority attribute-based encryption construction of Datta, Komargodski, and Waters (Journal of Cryptology, 2023). The attack succeeds in the claimed static model with one corrupt authority and two users whose individual attribute sets remain unauthorized even when combined with the corrupt authority's attribute. The flaw is an incorrect extension of LSSS matrix-normalization invariance from complete secret shares to coordinate-wise ciphertext masks. A corrupt authority can expose these masks and remove identity binding from other users' decryption shares. We replace the coordinate-wise masks with independent full linear sharings of zero and prove static security under decisional bilinear Diffie-Hellman (DBDH) in the random oracle model. The repair retains the original matrix-width and row-labeling restrictions and leaves authority keys, user keys, decryption, and ciphertext size unchanged, while increasing encryption randomness and field arithmetic. We also give analogous attacks on both multi-authority attribute-based inner-product functional encryption constructions of Datta and Pal (PKC, 2023). The same modification restores correctness and matrix-substitution invariance for both variants. We prove static security of the repaired small-universe variant under asymmetric DBDH. For the large-universe variant, we identify a separate missing source-group encoding in the original reduction, formulate an augmented $L$-DBDH assumption, prove its hardness in the asymmetric generic bilinear group model, and give a static security reduction for the repaired scheme.

title: When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models
author: Rushab Munot
abstract: Decision models return normalized probability distributions over candidate choices, which downstream applications can use to select among choices. Although their providers emphasize the reliability of these probabilities, calibration on tasks with a single correct choice does not establish their reliability when multiple choices are correct. We evaluate three decision models (Jev, Liquid d1, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions) on three diverse datasets (MetaTool, HotpotQA, and ECtHR) to study probability allocation and thresholding. Even when models rank every correct choice above every distractor, in 28% to 50% of those lists, at least one correct choice receives a probability below the uniform probability of 1/n, where n is the number of choices. We also present each model with five identical copies of a correct choice and observe probability disparities, with mean gaps ranging from 17 to 79 percentage points. We further show how these allocation disparities affect the recovery of multiple correct choices under probability thresholding. Decision-model probabilities can rank correct choices, but a probability threshold does not identify the set of correct choices.

title: norregel: a preregistered benchmark of dated numeric values in Norwegian law
author: Eirik Botten Nicolaysen
abstract: norregel asks language models for numeric values in Norwegian statutes, regulations and parliamentary decisions (NOK amounts, percentages, multiples of the National Insurance basic amount (G) and age limits), each at a stated date. The 916 items were extracted mechanically from Lovdata's open data, and each carries the dated history of its provision, so an answer can be classed as correct, outdated, wrong or uninterpretable. We report a first and a second preregistered run on the same items. In the first run (five models, listed publicly only after local analysis), H1, that outdated answers are more frequent for values that took effect after a model's cutoff, could not be tested in substance, and H2 and H3 were inconclusive; Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 4.6 answered 46.7% and 40.2% of the 880 primary items correctly. The second run was preregistered and published before any of its calls, and eight models were analysed. Its pooled primary test supported H1 under the preregistered decision rule (d = 17.8 percentage points, 95% interval [7.7, 28.9], p = 0.0001). In the preregistered sensitivity analysis S8, which counts as outdated only the most recent value that differs from the key, d was 3.9 [-3.6, 12.7] (p = 0.1754), an interval that contains 0. H1 was supported in every other preregistered sensitivity analysis, but S8 is the only one that gives both groups one target value, so we do not regard the support for H1 as robust. The share of outdated answers equal to that most recent value (H2) was 56.1% [46.6, 65.0], an interval that contains 0.5, and the pooled test of a lower share correct in Nynorsk than in Bokmål (H3) was inconclusive. Several models, among them Haiku 4.5, gave mostly uninterpretable answers. Items and keys are withheld; item IDs, per-answer classes, code and results are on Zenodo.

title: Truncated Out-of-Bag Probability Gain: A Noise-Robust Criterion for Random-Forest Wrapper Feature Selection
author: Sejong Oh
abstract: Random-Forest wrapper feature selection can use out-of-bag (OOB) predictions as a built-in validation signal, but the criteria that decide each forward step accumulate OOB estimation noise. We propose TOP-Gain (Truncated Out-of-bag Probability Gain), which scores a candidate feature by the mean sample-level increase in the OOB probability of the true class, with decreases truncated at zero. Under a simple noise model, truncation removes about two-thirds of the noise variance contributed by unaffected samples while preserving the signal, and it makes the ranking of candidate features markedly more reproducible. In a pre-registered benchmark on 26 OpenML-CC18 datasets, TOP-Gain achieved the best mean rank in area under the ROC curve (ROC-AUC), accuracy and Macro-F1 among 15 methods; it was significantly better than 13 of 14 baselines and matched the accuracy of VSURF with 21 times less single-core computation. Within an identical wrapper, it selected significantly more stable feature sets than net-gain, Brier, log-loss and accuracy criteria without loss of accuracy. A confirmatory study on 24 further datasets replicated the advantage over all baselines. The accuracy gains were broad rather than tied to specific dataset characteristics, and, as pre-registered, the stability gain grew as relevant features became sparser

title: Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors
author: Luca Zanolini
abstract: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.

title: Two for One: Privileged Learning for Resource-Constrained Screening
author: Lisa Y. W. Tang
abstract: Machine learning systems are often developed under data-rich conditions but deployed when only incomplete information is available. A natural example arises in colour fundus photography (CFP), where both eyes are commonly imaged because they can provide complementary information for ocular disease assessment. Prior approaches that exploit bilateral information either fuse both eyes in a single model or use knowledge distillation to compress a dual-eye teacher into a lightweight student that still requires both images at test time. However, bilateral acquisition may not always be feasible. We thus propose a privileged learning framework in which a teacher model has access to bilateral CFP images during training and learns representations informed by information from both eyes, while the student is trained to transfer this knowledge from the bilateral teacher using only a single-eye image as input. At inference, the student operates exclusively on this single-eye input and does not require the contralateral image. Experimental results show consistent improvements in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve over conventional monocular training, with the largest gains observed for left-eye images for the detection of age-related macular degeneration (0.931 vs. 0.966) and diabetic retinopathy (0.789 vs. 0.836).%, while requiring only a single-eye image at inference. By enabling models to benefit from bilateral information during training while requiring only a single-eye image at inference, our approach may support more reliable deployment in resource-constrained clinical and screening environments.

title: From Canon to Nikon: Camera Domain Shift and Potential Equity Implications in Retinal AI
author: Lisa Y. W. Tang
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness, yet access to regular screening remains limited worldwide. AI offers a scalable approach, but its performance can be sensitive to image quality and acquisition conditions. In a Brazilian cohort of 8,524 patients, retinal images acquired with the Nikon NF5050 were more than twice as likely to have inadequate image quality compared with those acquired with the Canon CR-2, despite refurbished Canon systems costing more than twice as much as Nikon systems. This potential cost-quality trade-off highlights an important consideration for the reliability of AI systems deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. Using a frozen pretrained retinal foundation model, we systematically evaluate whether camera-associated performance differences persist across 12 retinal disease classification tasks, four input resolutions, and five downstream classifiers. We find that camera-associated performance differences vary substantially across tasks, and that neither higher input resolution nor classifier choice consistently mitigates cross-camera variation. These findings identify camera platform as a potentially overlooked source of performance variability, with implications for the safety and reliability of retinal AI when deployed across heterogeneous imaging systems. We release all source code, evaluation scripts, and per-task results on GitHub to support reproducible benchmarking.

title: AMP Atlas: A Browser-Only Workbench for Antimicrobial Peptide Exploration and Interactive Helical-Wheel Design
author: Truong-Son Hy
abstract: Accessible research software can connect published antimicrobial peptide (AMP) records to sequence analysis, molecular visualization, and interactive design without requiring a dedicated application server. We present AMP Atlas, an open-source, browser-only workbench that combines a DRAMP-derived database with local physicochemical calculations, published-neighbor retrieval, and sequence-guided structural comparison. The reported snapshot contains 12,784 source records, 10,579 canonical records, 5,183 source SMILES annotations, and 433 PDB chain structures. An inverse helical-wheel editor lets users specify peptide length, fill residues gradually, and immediately retrieve exact-length database matches under positional and property constraints. Selected-position residue frequencies support further editing while preserving the remaining constraints. A Web Worker performs searches and numerical calculations; a WebGL viewer provides interactive molecular representations. The static distribution occupies 138.8 MB and supports GitHub Pages hosting. Verification includes 23 Python tests, 30 browser-core/worker checks, a designer DOM integration suite, and agreement against fixed numerical references. This report describes the implemented algorithms and assumptions; it does not establish predictive accuracy for antimicrobial activity or experimentally validate designed peptides. The website is available at https://hysonlab.github.io/amp-atlas/ and the source code and database are available at https://github.com/HySonLab/amp-atlas

title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation
author: Genpei Zhang
abstract: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.

title: Dynamics of Hidden Learning Structure
author: Qinyou Wang
abstract: A learner's present predictions do not fully determine how it will learn next. We study the dynamics of hidden learning structure through two related operations. Fiber Regulation Theory (FRT) describes protected repair of existing function and the learning responses left available after repair. Fiber Acquisition Theory (FAT) describes the formation and renewal of trainable structure, distinguishing neutral installation, access to a learning signal, and additional functional directions. The two operations also constrain one another. A repair obligation can force a change in a learning channel, while acquired features can make new protected repairs feasible or reduce the minimum coefficient cost of existing ones. We characterize joint admissibility and response reachability, and give a finite supervised-learning construction in which the two operations together produce a favorable response absent from either operation alone. We implement protected head repair and fixed-capacity LoRA renewal in Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, under replay and output distillation. Across two training trajectories differing in seed and within-task example order, the coordinated policy achieves higher teacher-forced Exact than either separate policy in all four comparisons. It also has the lowest macro NLL under both learning rules on the second trajectory. The implementations realize structure-conditioned self-regulation within specified information and action constraints: accessible state readouts and arrived evidence guide repairs and structural renewals, and ordinary learning continues from the modified state.

title: Resonance and Depth: Composing Timbral Identity and Spatial Form in an Artist-in-the-Loop Co-Creative Multi-Agent Percussive Performance
author: Keon Ju Maverick Lee
abstract: This research-creation artistic report presents Resonance and Depth, a 9-minute immersive electroacoustic/acousmatic performance that treats timbre and space as primary compositional materials. Built from live electronic percussion and a personal corpus recorded, curated, and composed by the author, the work investigates how timbral identity and musical form can emerge through real-time recombination, spatialisation, and performer-system interaction rather than conventional harmonic development. The performance is realised as an artist-in-the-loop co-creative multi-agent system integrating MACAT, MACataRT, a MIDI-based musical agent, a spatialisation layer, and a conductor agent. These components recombine and transform the performer's material through concatenative synthesis, audio mosaicing, symbolic mediation, physically inspired synthesis, and object-based spatialisation. The work approaches spatialisation as an active compositional process in which position, trajectory, depth, diffusion, width, and apparent size participate in musical phrasing and form. Through this practice-based framework, Resonance and Depth examines how performer identity can be retained, transformed, and redistributed across human, algorithmic, timbral, and spatial processes within an immersive co-creative performance ecology.

title: Single-Image Food Mass Estimators Do Not Transfer Their Gram Scale Across Datasets
author: Yongsheng Lian
abstract: Estimating food mass from a photograph is central to image-based dietary assessment, but whether trained models transfer to new cameras and foods is unclear. We fine-tuned DINOv2-base on 2,253 weighed Nutrition5k dishes to predict mass from one RGB photograph and compared it with a zero-shot vision-language model, Qwen3-VL-32B, on Nutrition5k and three external datasets: ASA24 studio portions, ECUSTFD whole foods and Food Portion Benchmark meal trays. In domain, the fine-tuned model's mean absolute error was 24.8 g, less than half of Qwen's. On external datasets it did not beat Qwen. For a food it had never seen, it ranked portions by size, but no better than a count of food pixels. Its gram scale was wrong in two ways: it changed with how much of the scene the photograph showed, and it was off by a different factor for each food. Training on other foods or trays from the tested dataset cut the external error by 38 to 65%. DINOv2-large, a larger backbone trained on the same dishes, did not reduce the external error. One labeled photograph of the same food cut the model's ASA24 error to 28.3 g, better than that photograph achieved alone. Prediction intervals that held the true mass for 90% of Nutrition5k dishes held it for at most half of external photographs. Nutrition5k often photographed the same plate several times, so a random test split shared near-identical photographs with training and overstated accuracy. Single-image mass estimators therefore need labeled photographs from the setting where they are used.

title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
author: Xiuyi Qin
abstract: NVIDIA tensor cores have supported 2:4 semi-structured sparsity since Ampere, and the pattern composes with quantization. When the two are combined, the practical question is which step to take next: from a given precision, add 2:4 sparsity or drop to the next lower precision? We compare the two at equal bits, with sparsity metadata counted, and at equal nominal tensor-core tiers, over all six GEMM operands of a transformer layer, with kernels measured on three GPU generations and online pruning and quantization included. Our results show that as long as a lower precision is available, adding 2:4 is the worse step, both less accurate and slower, because the energy that 2:4 discards from each group of four along the hardware-forced axis does not shrink with bits, while quantization error does. Once quantization reaches the lowest precision the hardware supports, 2:4 still speeds up linear layers by 1.3--1.7\x{}, and on an H100 a retrained 2:4 model served in FP8 by vLLM reaches 27\% higher prefill throughput than the dense FP8 model, with GSM8K accuracy on par. Its quality has to be won back by retraining, however, which restores perplexity long before reasoning; on Blackwell, whose sparse FP4 uses a pairwise 4:8 pattern, the loss is larger and our retraining budget did not recover it.

title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
author: Qin Xin
abstract: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted; collision detection is unavailable. Our protocol combines amplified reception certificates, adaptive pruning, and permutation selectors. Each pruning iteration costs $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. A two-step quadratic contraction limits each receiver and each class of identical closed in-neighborhoods to $\mathcal O(\log\log n)$ qualifying selections. Under an explicit degree-concentration condition, our protocol takes $\mathcal O(m\log^2n(\log\log n)^2)$ rounds. For directed regular graphs with common in- and out-degree $Δ$, our strategy achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrtΔ,n^2/Δ\})$, extending the identifier range of Wu and Chrobak and improving their high-degree bound. At completion entry, let $a\ge1$ count original sources not yet credited as globally disseminated. Permutation selectors reduce our balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. Our geometric protocol attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+nτ+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for an original path cover of scale $k$, weight $τ$, and $u$ exceptions. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs. Within the stated graph classes and identifier ranges, these results answer the polynomial-identifier and average-degree questions of Wu and Chrobak. The unrestricted general-graph cases remain open.

title: An algorithmic construction of Nullstellensatz certificates for graph automorphism groups
author: Ivan Drecun
abstract: Solvers for graph isomorphism and related problems are widely used in both theoretical and applied domains, but their complexity often requires users to trust their correctness without verification. We present a certifying algorithm for computing a generating set of the automorphism group of a given graph, meaning that it produces an independently verifiable certificate that the output list of automorphisms generates the entirety of the automorphism group. The problem of constructing a certificate is reduced to certifying that a system of multivariate polynomial equations is infeasible. An individualization-refinement algorithm produces a derivation within an algebraic proof system, representing a Nullstellensatz certificate of infeasibility. We provide an implementation of both the certifying algorithm and a certificate verifier, and demonstrate their viability on graphs with hundreds of vertices.

title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
author: Jose M. Peña
abstract: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.

title: Is Refusal Direction Universal across Low-Resourced Languages?
author: Anastasiia Ivanova
abstract: Refusal directions have been shown to transfer cross-lingually with near-perfect effectiveness across safety-aligned languages (Wang et al., 2025), reportedly regardless of resource level. However, the only truly low-resourced language evaluated is Yoruba, which is strongly misaligned and shows limited transfer, leaving open how refusal directions behave for other low-resourced languages. We extend PolyRefuse to three additional low-resourced languages (Belarusian, Bashkir, and Tajik) and replicate the pipeline of (Wang et al., 2025) on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. We find that universality is graded rather than binary: directions from safety-aligned and partially-aligned languages transfer broadly, while those from strongly misaligned languages fail to reliably modulate refusal behavior on any target tested, including other misaligned languages, once ceiling effects are accounted for. Geometric alignment and behavioral transfer are further shown to be partially dissociated. These findings complicate the universality claim and suggest that users of the least-resourced, most strongly misaligned languages may face weaker safety guarantees.

title: How Much Gradient Does Truncated Backprop Lose in Looped Transformers?
author: Aur Shalev Merin
abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops. We measure how much of the weight gradient this throws away, exactly and for every k from one backward pass, on nine looped language models, and report three findings. First, on a trained model this lost gradient is set near the output: once the loop count is well above k, it barely changes with the loop count (within about 0.03 from 32 to 64 loops on the three models we tested, as a pre-registered test predicted for Parcae). Where the backward signal shrinks, $ρ^k$, with $ρ$ the signal's fitted shrink per loop, approximates it at moderate loop counts but overstates it at long ones, because the fitted $ρ$ drifts up as the fit takes in more loops. On Ouro the signal grows, and keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient. Second, the lost gradient falls during fine-tuning, by 0.07-0.22 within 300 steps on three of four models, on held-out problems too. The fall is not just the read-out's share of the gradient; training only the layers outside the loop reproduced up to half of it, and it also falls under truncated training. So a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. Third, we could not show that it predicts the training cost of truncation better than rules that need no measurement: on two new models it tied Parcae's cost at the same k, in a test too small to separate them.

title: A General Topological Symmetry Index for Critical Orbits In Neural Network Loss Landscapes
author: Jingzhou Liu
abstract: A systematic understanding of the global structure of neural-network loss landscapes remains challenging due to their high dimensionality. Symmetries arising from network architectures and learning objectives provide a way to investigate aspects of this structure. Although a growing number of studies have drawn attention to these symmetries, a systematic characterization of them, as well as of the critical orbits they give rise to, remains incomplete. To address this gap, in this work we establish a topological symmetry index, based on the methodologies from the family of equivariant degree theories, to decode these symmetries. The frameworks apply to arbitrary network architectures and include methods applicable to degenerate critical orbits. The index detects the isotropy of the critical points and quantifies the corresponding net topological contributions. Several examples, including softplus MLPs, Transformers, and equivariant neural networks, are presented to illustrate the computations.

title: Agent AI Zarządzający Siecią Open RAN Zorientowana na Użytkownika
author: Marcin Hoffmann
abstract: Jednym z najważniejszych wyzwań związanych z implementacją sieci Open RAN o architekturze zorientowanej na użytkownika jest odpowiednie formowanie tzw. klastrów obsługujących. Problem ten może być efektywnie rozwiązany za pomocą zaproponowanego Agenta AI bazującego na modelu językowym. Wyniki symulacji pokazały, że zaproponowane rozwiązanie pozwala na ponad 2-krotne zwiększenie mediany rozkładu przepływności użytkowników względem standardowej architektury zorientowanej na sieć.

title: When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning
author: Wang Ru
abstract: Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space. For base generation this default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, however, it carries a structural limitation. The standard VAE's KL term does not merely ignore mode structure - it actively taxes separation and tightness. When data are multimodal, the ELBO optimum compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, dynamic-to-variational amplification rises sharply, and the collapse boundary beta_c is pushed far above its variational scale. On the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at beta_c = 0.224 while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior collapses at 0.00316, a 71x gap from the same pipeline. We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d_min/(2 sigma_0), and verify the causal chain through controlled interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995x, 95% CI [0.79, 1.25]). A three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution, bounded anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no amount of RL capacity recovers. The remedy is conditional: a non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would fall into overlap and the task is coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton supports the KL pricing structure - a divergent compactness tax under a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture - and the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource from what requires changing the prior.

title: Towards Realistic Models of Change: A Causal Perspective on Decision-Making and Dynamical Systems
author: Isacco Beretta
abstract: While statistical learning has made remarkable progress in recent decades, driven by large datasets and data-driven protocols that have transformed scientific practice, it still faces a key limitation: it struggles to generalize beyond the data it has seen, often failing under distribution shift. Causality offers a promising solution: causal models focus on the underlying mechanisms of change rather than surface-level associations, enabling robust reasoning under external interventions. This allows systems not only to learn from data, but also to reason about hypothetical scenarios, adapt to new environments, and inform better decisions. This thesis explores how these approaches can inform each other, in two parts. The first part examines algorithmic recourse, that is, identifying which changes an individual can make to overturn an unfavorable decision.
